description: Reichstag Fire, Enabling Act, Night of the Long Knives — dictatorship in eighteen months.
content_html:
From Chancellor to Dictator

When Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933, he did not yet have dictatorial power. Germany was still a constitutional republic. He had only two other Nazis in his twelve-man cabinet, and President Hindenburg retained the power to dismiss him. Within eighteen months, Hitler had eliminated all rivals, abolished all other political parties, and fused the offices of Chancellor and President. The speed and completeness of this transformation shocked even those who had expected him to be radical.

The Reichstag Fire and Emergency Decree, February 1933

On the night of 27 February 1933, the Reichstag building was set on fire. A young Dutch communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, was found at the scene and arrested. Hitler immediately blamed the Communist Party for an organised plot to overthrow the state. Within hours, he had persuaded President Hindenburg to sign the Reichstag Fire Decree, which suspended freedom of speech, assembly, and the press, and allowed the police to arrest and detain anyone without trial. The communists were effectively outlawed. Over the following days, thousands of political opponents were arrested.

Key Fact

The Enabling Act (23 March 1933) passed by 444 votes to 94, with the SA lining the chamber. It gave Hitler the power to pass laws without the Reichstag's approval for four years — effectively making him a dictator within the bounds of the constitution.

The Enabling Act, March 1933

On 23 March 1933, the Reichstag voted on the Enabling Act. For it to pass, Hitler needed a two-thirds majority. He achieved this by having communist deputies arrested and by surrounding the Reichstag with SA stormtroopers to intimidate the remaining members. Only the Social Democrats voted against — their leader Otto Wels delivered a courageous speech defending democracy, knowing it would make no difference. The act passed by 444 votes to 94. Hitler now had the legal power to govern by decree.

Gleichschaltung (co-ordination) swept through German society over the following months. State governments were abolished and replaced by Nazi-appointed Reich governors. Trade unions were banned and replaced by the Nazi-controlled German Labour Front in May 1933. All political parties except the Nazis were dissolved or forced to disband by July 1933. Germany became a one-party state.

By 1934, the SA had grown to over two million members and its leader, Ernst Röhm, was demanding that the SA absorb the regular army and lead a ‘second revolution’ that would redistribute wealth. This alarmed conservative generals and industrialists whose support Hitler needed. On the night of 29–30 June 1934, the SS carried out mass arrests and executions across Germany. Röhm was murdered, as were many other SA leaders and political opponents, including former Chancellor Schleicher. Estimates of those killed range from several dozen to several hundred.

The Night of the Long Knives had two crucial effects. First, it destroyed the SA as an independent political force — it was subordinated to the SS and effectively domesticated. Second, it showed the German army that Hitler would protect their institutional interests, which secured military loyalty. The generals accepted what had happened because it served their own interests.

Key Fact

When President Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934, Hitler merged the offices of President and Chancellor, taking the title Führer (leader). The German army swore a personal oath of loyalty to Hitler as an individual — not to the German state or constitution — binding every soldier to him personally.

On 2 August 1934, President Hindenburg died. Within hours, Hitler announced that the offices of Chancellor and President had been merged into the new title of Führer. A plebiscite held on 19 August 1934 gave Hitler 89.9% of the vote in approval — though the conditions under which it was held made a free vote impossible. The personal oath of loyalty sworn by the army meant that any resistance to Hitler was now not merely illegal but a personal betrayal of a sacred vow. In just eighteen months, Hitler had dismantled the entire Weimar constitutional framework and concentrated all power in his own hands.

The speed of this consolidation is worth emphasising for exam purposes. Hitler exploited every crisis and opportunity methodically: the Reichstag Fire gave him a pretext to arrest communists before the March elections; the Enabling Act gave him legal cover for dictatorship; Gleichschaltung dismantled every independent institution before opposition could organise; and the Night of the Long Knives eliminated internal rivals while securing the loyalty of the one institution — the army — that could theoretically have stopped him. Each step was legally dressed in constitutional language even as it destroyed constitutional norms. This use of ‘legal revolution’ was precisely what Hitler had drawn from the failure of the Munich Putsch in 1923: raw force alone was insufficient; he needed the appearance of legitimacy to neutralise conservative resistance until it was too late to matter.
exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘Explain change’ question on how Germany’s political system changed between January 1933 and August 1934, structure your answer around the key turning points: the Reichstag Fire Decree (February 1933), the Enabling Act (March 1933), the Night of the Long Knives (June 1934), and Hindenburg’s death (August 1934). Don’t just list these events — explain how each one moved Germany further from democracy and closer to one-man dictatorship.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Reichstag Fire (February 1933) gave Hitler the pretext to suspend civil liberties via the Reichstag Fire Decree; the Enabling Act (March 1933) gave him legal power to govern without the Reichstag.
  • Gleichschaltung co-ordinated German institutions under Nazi control; trade unions were banned and all political parties except the NSDAP were dissolved by July 1933.
  • The Night of the Long Knives (June 1934) destroyed the SA as an independent force; Hindenburg’s death (August 1934) allowed Hitler to become Führer and receive the army’s personal oath of loyalty, completing the dictatorship.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Enabling Act of March 1933.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (2): identifies a specific feature with precise detail (e.g. gave Hitler the power to pass laws without Reichstag approval for four years; required a two-thirds majority to pass). Secure (1–2): feature identified with some detail. Developing (1): vague reference to Hitler gaining power. Emerging (0–1): no relevant detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the process by which Hitler consolidated power between January and July 1933.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4): two features each with precise detail — e.g. the Reichstag Fire Decree (February 1933) suspended civil liberties and enabled mass arrests of communists; the Enabling Act (March 1933) gave Hitler power to govern by decree for four years. Secure (3): two features with development. Developing (2): two features briefly stated. Emerging (1): one feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Night of the Long Knives in June 1934.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear cause (e.g. Röhm's demands that the SA replace the regular army threatened Hitler's relationship with conservative generals and industrialists he needed; OR: Hitler needed to destroy the SA as an independent political power base that challenged his own authority) with specific evidence and link to the purge. Secure (3–4): cause identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Night of the Long Knives for the Nazi regime.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): clear consequence (e.g. the SA was destroyed as an independent force and subordinated to the SS; the army's loyalty was secured because Hitler had protected its institutional position; conservatives who had feared a SA 'second revolution' were reassured) with specific evidence and further effects. Secure (3–4): consequence identified and developed. Developing (2): brief explanation. Emerging (1): vague mention.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the political system in Germany changed in the period from January 1933 to August 1934.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): tracks change at multiple points — January 1933 (Hitler Chancellor, constitutional position, coalition cabinet), Reichstag Fire Decree, Enabling Act, Gleichschaltung (trade unions, parties dissolved), Night of the Long Knives, August 1934 Führer, army oath — with analysis of HOW change occurred at each stage. Secure (5–6): covers most stages with development. Developing (3–4): some stages covered but limited analysis of process of change. Emerging (1–2): broadly describes the outcome without tracking change.

practice_questions.text: 'The Enabling Act of March 1933 was the most important step in Hitler's consolidation of power.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): agreement (Enabling Act gave legal foundation for dictatorship, bypassed democratic checks, enabled all subsequent legislation) AND disagreement (Reichstag Fire Decree came first and was equally enabling; Night of the Long Knives eliminated internal Nazi rivals and secured army; Hindenburg's death and the Führer oath completed the process). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7–9): both sides developed; judgement present. Developing (4–6): one side stronger; limited judgement. Emerging (1–3): mainly descriptive.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Reichstag Fire Decree allow?
flashcard_questions.a: Suspension of civil liberties and arrest of political opponents without trial.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Enabling Act passed, and by what vote?

flashcard_questions.a: The Nazi process of 'co-ordination' — forcing all institutions and organisations to conform to Nazi control.

flashcard_questions.q: When were trade unions banned and replaced by the German Labour Front?
When were all political parties except the NSDAP dissolved?
flashcard_questions.a: July 1933, making Germany a one-party state.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was Ernst Röhm and why was he killed?
flashcard_questions.a: SA leader killed on the Night of the Long Knives (June 1934) because his demands threatened Hitler's alliance with the army.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Night of the Long Knives take place?
When did Hindenburg die, and what did Hitler do on the same day?
flashcard_questions.a: 2 August 1934 — Hitler merged Chancellor and President into the title Führer.

flashcard_questions.q: What oath did the German army swear on 2 August 1934?
flashcard_questions.a: A personal oath of loyalty to Hitler as an individual, not to the state or constitution.

flashcard_questions.q: What percentage voted in favour of Hitler becoming Führer in the August 1934 plebiscite?

glossary_terms.definition: Germany's parliamentary building, which was set on fire on 27 February 1933 — an event that Hitler used as a pretext to suspend civil liberties.
An emergency decree signed by President Hindenburg on 28 February 1933 that suspended civil liberties and allowed the arrest of political opponents without trial.
A law passed on 23 March 1933 that gave Hitler the power to make laws without Reichstag approval for four years, effectively making him a legal dictator.
The Nazi process of 'co-ordination' — forcing German institutions, regional governments, trade unions and civic organisations to conform to Nazi ideology and come under central control.
Leader of the SA (Brownshirts) until he was killed on the Night of the Long Knives in June 1934; he wanted the SA to replace the regular army.
The German title meaning 'leader', which Hitler adopted in August 1934 when he merged the offices of Chancellor and President into a single all-powerful role.
